sources: Great Lakes Fishery Commission, Sea Lamprey: no jaws, cartilage skeleton; a large oral sucking disk filled with sharp horn-shaped teeth around a razor-sharp rasping tongue; attaches and rasps through scales and skin, secreting an enzyme that stops blood clotting like a leech; each can kill up to 40 lb of fish in its 12-18 month feeding period; largely unchanged for more than 340 million years, survived at least four major extinctions; first recorded in Lake Ontario 1835, Welland Canal improvements let it past Niagara Falls into Lake Erie by 1921 and Lake Superior by 1938; lake trout catch fell from about 15 million lb a year to about 300,000 lb; up to 85 percent of surviving fish bore lamprey wounds; https://www.glfc.org/sea-lamprey.php

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Sea Lamprey: larvae develop in stream sediment for about four to 17 years; a female can produce up to 100,000 eggs; females die soon after spawning, males within one to three days; https://www.fws.gov/midwest/SeaLamprey/

beats.say: This fish latches on to other fish, and drinks their blood.
So I shrank myself down, to get a closer look at that mouth.
The sea lamprey. No jaws, and no bones. Just cartilage.
Its mouth is a round sucking disk, packed with sharp teeth, and a razor tongue.
It latches on, and grinds right through the scales and skin.
Then it oozes a chemical that stops the blood from clotting.
So, a leech. But it's a fish. And it's two feet long.
One lamprey can kill up to forty pounds of fish.
Its babies hide in the mud at the bottom of a stream, for four to seventeen years.
About a hundred years ago, a ship canal let it past Niagara Falls, into the Great Lakes.
The lake trout catch crashed by about ninety-eight percent.
At the worst, most of the fish that survived an attack had lamprey wounds.
And this design is ancient. Over three hundred forty million years, barely changed.
It survived at least four mass extinctions.
One female can lay up to a hundred thousand eggs. And then she dies.
Would you swim in a lake with these?
Older than dinosaurs, tougher than extinctions, and it still eats like a vampire.
Follow me. Next, an ant that's actually a wasp, with a sting they call the cow killer.
